sources.cite: AWS documentation (Route 53), How Amazon Route 53 chooses records when health checking is configured
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-18. 'Records without a health check are always healthy': 'If a record in a group of records that have the same name and type doesn't have an associated health check, Route 53 always considers it healthy'; for failover records, 'If Route 53 considers the primary record unhealthy and the secondary record healthy, Route 53 returns the secondary record'. The failover record values page (resource-record-sets-values-failover.html, read the same day) advises 'a TTL of 60 seconds or less' with health checks.

brief.situation: You are the network engineer at Caldera Tours. book.caldera.example uses Route 53 failover routing: a primary record for the us-east-1 web tier and a secondary for the warm standby in us-west-2. Since 17:50 the us-east-1 tier returns errors after a bad deploy, and the standby is healthy, but DNS still answers with us-east-1. The evening flash sale opens at 19:00.
handover: The records were migrated from another DNS provider last month by a script.
The standby in us-west-2 was tested last week and serves the full site.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the failover record pair, the health check that should drive it, and the two web tiers.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why DNS did not fail over, what you changed, and how failover is kept working.

parts.label: Why
parts.modelAnswer: The migrated primary record had no health check; Route 53 considers a record without a health check always healthy, so it kept answering with the failing east tier.

parts.label: Changed
parts.modelAnswer: Created an HTTPS health check on the east tier's /health, attached it to the primary and set the TTL to 60; DNS moved to us-west-2. A simple record with a day-long TTL removes failover; restarting the east tier reapplies the bad deploy.

parts.label: Kept working
parts.modelAnswer: A check on the standby, an alarm on the primary's health status, and a monthly failover test.

failoverGone.headline: Keep the failover; give it a health check
failoverGone.body: Failover routing works when the primary has a health check. Replacing it with a long-TTL simple record trades one outage for the next.

saleDown.headline: A record with no health check is always healthy
saleDown.body: Route 53 fails over only when it considers the primary unhealthy. Without a health check, it never does.

failedOver.headline: Good: failover driven by health
failedOver.body: You read the record pair, saw the primary had no health check, confirmed the standby was healthy, attached a health check with a short TTL, verified the answer changed, and added alarms and a failover test.

scoring.modelReasoning: Failover routing only fails over when the primary is unhealthy, and the primary record has no health check, so Route 53 always treats it as healthy. With the standby confirmed healthy, create a health check on the east tier, attach it to the primary and shorten the TTL, then check DNS answers with us-west-2. A long-TTL simple record removes failover; restarting reapplies the bad deploy. Then alarm on health and test failover regularly.
